title: Henrietta Szold
hookLine: teacher of immigrants and founder of Hadassah

lines: A TEACHER WITH CHALK ON HER FINGERS.
cards: Evening in Baltimore. The workday is done, and a classroom fills up with adults: tailors, peddlers, factory hands, newly arrived, still in their work clothes, tired to the bone. They've come to learn English.

At the front stands a young woman with chalk on her fingers, a rabbi's daughter who teaches by day as well. She hands out the books and starts with the alphabet. Her name is Henrietta Szold, and today she's the word.

teach.b: Henrietta Szold grew up in Baltimore, the daughter of a rabbi, and became a teacher.

When refugees from the pogroms began arriving in her city, she helped start a night school for them, teaching English and the ways of a new country to people who worked all day. Then she taught in another way: with a pen.
She worked for years as an editor at the Jewish Publication Society, preparing books for American Jewish readers, the same society whose English Bible this path quotes.
Then a journey changed her direction. She traveled to the land of Israel, then under Ottoman rule, and saw sickness and poverty there, especially among mothers and children.
She came home and, with a group of women, founded an organization to send nurses and build care. They named it Hadassah.
In the book of Esther, the queen has two names: the text calls her "Hadassah, that is, Esther." Esther was the one who spoke up for her people when it counted.

Late in life, Szold moved to the land of Israel herself, and in the dark years of Nazi Germany she helped lead the work of bringing Jewish children out to safety, and then making sure they were cared for and taught.
The Torah puts it plainly, in the passage Jews say morning and evening: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Szold took that verse wide. Immigrants were her children.
Readers were her children. Rescued children were her children. Teach, in every room she entered.

how: Jews say the Shema with its line about teaching the commandments to your children in morning and evening prayers, and Hadassah still runs medical, education and volunteer work today.

practice: Bring back one thing someone once taught you that you still use: how to tie a knot, a word in another language, a recipe. See the person who taught it, how patient they were, and hold them with thanks for a few breaths.
